entries.title: Houthi advances in Yemen drive displacement, deepen humanitarian crisis
entries.summary: With more than 132,000 people already displaced by the latest fighting and Houthi territorial gains, Yemen is on the brink of slipping back into a full-fledged humanitarian emergency. DW spoke with people on the ground.
entries.content:
Yemen

Yemen's Saudi-Houthi conflict fuels humanitarian crisis

September 24, 2026

With more than 132,000 people already displaced by the latest fighting and Houthi territorial gains, Yemen is on the brink of slipping back into a full-fledged humanitarian emergency. DW spoke with people on the ground.

Mohammed Musleh is still in shock. Following the Houthi capture of the port town of Mokha earlier in September, his family had to flee their home without time to pack.

"We have no idea what will happen now," the 46-year-old told DW. His wife, Muna, is also worried, as the family couldn't bring their personal identification documents. "The Houthis told us to leave, basically immediately. We had no time to take anything," she said.

For now, the family and their two young daughters are staying with relatives in Aden, the largest city controlled by the government in southern Yemen. "We tell our kids in the meantime that we hope to return home soon," the couple said.

Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of the Presidential Council, the leadership body of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, said that recent battlefield changes would not alter the government's goal of restoring state authority nationwide.

However, given the latest advances by the Iran-backed Houthis and their territorial gains in Yemen, a return of the Musleh family to their home in Mokha is unlikely for now.

Since late July, the Iran-backed Houthis have expanded their areas of control from the north and center of the country to much of Yemen's Red Sea coast, seizing territory from forces of the internationally recognized and Saudi-backed government. The conflict continues to escalate, along with an exchange of missile and drone attacks between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis are currently pushing further into the country toward the strategic Kahboub Mountains. The mountain range is significant as it overlooks areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key waterway that had been serving as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports amid Iran's blockade of the nearby Strait of Hormuz.

Staying at home or leaving Taiz?

The mountains are also only around 40 kilometers (25 miles) southwest of Taiz, which is under government control.

Fatima, a mother in Taiz, has been telling her children that the sounds of shelling are from fireworks. "We are scared and we are also worried as gas has already become unavailable and prices are rising. Merchants are no longer coming into Taiz," she told DW, asking not to publish her full name for fear of reprisal.

Rania and her children have also decided to stay at home in Taiz for now. "But we fear that if the Houthis tighten their grip on the city of Taiz, we will find ourselves under siege again," she said. She also doesn't want to use her first name, and vividly recalls the "suffocating blockade of 2015 and 2016, when the entry of food and goods was cut off."

During the previous war between the Iran-aligned Houthi group and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, which began in 2014 and largely ended with a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022, Houthi forces blocked most routes into the government-controlled city of Taiz for almost two years. The restrictions on food, medical supplies and humanitarian aid drove up prices and left people on the brink of famine.

Growing displacement numbers

The World Health Organization said this week that at least 674 people have been killed and 2,998 injured since fighting escalated in August. However, due to the ongoing clashes, the death tally may already be higher, as fighting is ongoing.

The conflict has also prompted mass displacement of more than 132,000 people, according to the International Organization for Migration. In recent days, more than 90,000 people found refuge in Aden, Lahj, Abyan and Al Dhale'e governorates and even in Marib, the UN refugee agency's Yemen representative Armen Yedgaryan saidon Tuesday.

He also predicted that intensifying fighting could drive more mass displacement, with growing numbers of people expected to flee to Djibouti, Somalia and other countries, as well as within Yemen.

"Conditions for displaced people are increasingly severe as they arrive at already congested displacement sites in urgent need of shelter, food, clean water, healthcare and protection, placing additional pressure on fragile services and infrastructure," he said.

Even before the latest escalation, more than 5.2 million people were internally displaced in Yemen, and the current fighting is deepening an already dire humanitarian crisis in the country, the UN refugee agency added.

Around 22 million people require humanitarian assistance, including internally displaced people and around 65,000 refugees and asylum-seekers, mainly from Somalia and Ethiopia.

Displaced Yemenis help other displaced Yemenis

"I was in the Al-Kud site, a camp for internally displaced people or IDPs, in Abyan governorate on Sunday," said Alison Bottomley, an advocacy adviser with the Norwegian Refugee Council in Yemen, adding that "317 families have arrived since the fighting began, increasing the number of people from 1,460 to 2,629 people."

However, there is no funding to support them. "These IDPs are surviving purely off the generosity of other IDP families."

She told DW that she met Mustapha, a man who was displaced from his hometown of Mawza seven years ago during the previous war in Yemen. He has been living at the IDP site ever since. "He told us he was hosting 22 families in his shelter, all people from his hometown in Mawza. Together, they share a single latrine. When I asked how they were all eating, he said they share one meal together every other day."

Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, meanwhile, released a video message in which he told Yemenis in western and southern provinces that they are not the target.

However, Yemeni political analyst Hisham Al-Omeisy said these are empty words.

"The Houthis may measure this offensive in kilometers gained and territory seized, but Yemenis are measuring it in homes abandoned, families torn apart, and lives lost," he told DW.

"There is something profoundly cruel about pursuing military gains while ordinary Yemenis are once again being condemned to fear, hunger and displacement," Al-Omeisy said, adding that "the lines on the map may change, but the blood, grief and shattered lives behind those lines belong to real people. Yemen's civilians cannot continue to be treated as collateral damage in the Houthis' pursuit of power."

Edited by: Andreas Illmer

entries.title: Nigeria, US agree to boost mining investment on sidelines of UN General Assembly
entries.summary: On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Nigeria and the US inked a new mining deal. Nigeria is home to deposits of lithium, gold, tin, gemstones, iron ore and phosphate.
entries.content:
September 24, 2026

On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Nigeria and the US inked a new mining deal. Nigeria is home to deposits of lithium, gold, tin, gemstones, iron ore and phosphate.

Nigeria and the US have agreed to "deepen" American investment in the West African country's mining sector.

The deal was signed on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York City, Nigeria's Minister for Solid Minerals Dele Alake announced on Thursday.

"This is an important step in strengthening Nigeria-US cooperation around our mineral resources, valued at about $700 billion (€796 billion)," Alake said.

"The framework covers geological data and exploration, mineral development and processing, infrastructure, and technical capacity,"he added.

'We want more local processing'

Although known for its vast oil reserves, Nigeria is also home to deposits of lithium, gold, tin, gemstones, iron ore and phosphate.

Lithium, in particular, is in high demand globally as an essential component in the batteries are powering the green energy transition.

Alake said the agreement, which was signed on Wednesday, would be used to identify viable projects. He hinted that local jobs could be created by onshoring the refining of minerals, which until now have largely been exported as ore.

"Nigeria cannot remain a source of raw materials while others capture most of the value," Alake said. "We want more local processing, quality jobs, stronger skills and greater opportunities for Nigerian businesses."

However, these goals come as Nigeria's mining sector remains mired by safety concerns and environmental concerns.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: UNGA: Abbas blasts US and Israel, calls for Palestinian self-determination
entries.summary: At the UN General Assembly, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas urged nations to support the two-state solution. He stated that his people seek a democratic Palestinian state that can coexist with Israel. DW has more.
entries.content:
Published September 22, 2026last updated September 24, 2026

At the UN General Assembly, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas urged nations to support the two-state solution. He stated that his people seek a democratic Palestinian state that can coexist with Israel. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas urged nations to support the two-state solution
  • Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has arrived in New York with protests expected at the UN
  • The UK will host a meeting on the future of the Gaza Strip, while Saudi Arabia and Norway have called a ministerial meeting to discuss the implementation of the so-called two-state solution
  • Beyond the Middle East, day 3 of the UNGA will address the problem that rising sea levels pose for low-lying islands and coastal regions

Read below for all the top headlines, videos and analyses on the 81 UN General Assembly from September 22-28, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section READ: Nigeria and US sign mining deal

READ: Nigeria and US sign mining deal

On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Nigeria and the United States agreed to increase American investiment in the West African nation's mining sector.

Nigeria's Minister for Solid Minerals Dele Alake announced the deal on Thursday, a day after he signed the framework deal with US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau.

"Nigeria cannot remain a source of raw materials while others capture most of the value. We want more local processing, quality jobs, stronger skills and greater opportunities for Nigerian businesses," Alake said.

Read more about the US-Nigeria mining agreement.

Skip next section Abbas calls for saving two-state solution and Palestinian self-determination

Abbas calls for saving two-state solution and Palestinian self-determination

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas used his remarks to implore nations to support the two-state solution, saying his people seek a non-militarized, democratic Palestinian state that can exist alongside Israel in peace.

He said the first step to preserving the idea of such a solution is to protect the lands upon which a future Palestinian state would be based, as well as protecting those people who have lived upon them for generations.

Abbas underscored the fact that the Palestinian people would not be displaced by "military occupation, nor settlement expansion, annexation, nor settler terrorism."

He further said that "no lasting security can be built upon the occupation of another people and the denial of its legitimate rights," adding that the Palestinians have their own plans for an independent state and emphasizing the need to end the Israeli occupation in order to negotiate a solution.

This plan, Abbas said, is based on protecting Palestinians from displacement, preserving their lands, democratically renewing political institutions and building a new sovereign Palestinian state — with east Jerusalem as its capital.

All of this, he said, would be carried out with a "commitment to international law" and the right to exercise self-determination with the aim of achieving security and peace with Israel to, "pave the way to regional integration, cooperation, prosperity and security for everyone."

Abbas concluded his remarks by thanking those 160 nations whom he said have recognized Palestinian statehood, calling for its inclusion in the United Nations.

Skip next section Palestinian leader Abbas blasts US and Israel in General Assembly

Palestinian leader Abbas blasts US and Israel in General Assembly

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, addressing those gathered at the UNGA via video because the US State Department refused to allow the Palestinian delegation into the country, has rejected Washington's approach as "unlawful and punitive."

Abbas described the denial of visas as a US failure to live up to its responsibility as the host nation of the international body.

Abbas quickly pivoted to blast Israel's "genocidal war" in Gaza, as well as the sanctioned "ethnic cleansing" perpetrated by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.

Saying that Israeli violations of international law put the two-state solution at grave risk, Abbas described the situation in Gaza, the West Bank and east Jerusalem as part of a "malicious colonial scheme" and warned of a "new Nakba."

He also referenced attacks on Muslim and Christian religious sites by radical Jews as having the potential to transform the current security situation into a wider religiously fueled conflict.

Skip next section Not only Middle East, rising sea level threat also on slate for day 3 meetings

Not only Middle East, rising sea level threat also on slate for day 3 meetings

Beyond AI and the headline-grabbing conflict in the Middle East, the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday will discuss another pressing issue that impacts the world’s citizens — rising sea levels.

A high-level meeting is slated to begin at 10:00 a.m. (1400 GMT) on Thursday as swelling seas redraw coastlines and pose existential risks for islanders and those who live in low-lying areas near the shores of the world's oceans and seas.

The UN says nearly 900 million people live in such areas, adding that another one million could be impacted by mid-century.

Rising sea levels, says the UN, threaten not only land but also livelihoods and even the existence of entire nations. In the words of UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, "Rising seas are sinking futures."

Skip next section Israeli and Palestinian leaders set to address UNGA on day 3

Israeli and Palestinian leaders set to address UNGA on day 3

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas are both expected to address members of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) on Thursday, with the issue of the Middle East writ large on the day 3 agenda.

Netanyahu, who is increasingly unpopular at home and abroad, will not meet with US officials or Arab leaders during his stay. His office cited a "tight schedule" as the reason, listing as many as nine meetings during his visit, including with the presidents of Argentina and Bolivia, the vice president of Colombia and the prime minister of Papua New Guinea.

The increasingly isolated Israeli leader's Palestinian counterpart, President Mahmoud Abbas, will also address the General Assembly. Abbas, however, will do so via video, as the US State Department refused to issue him an entry visa.

The broader subjects of Gaza's future and Palestinian statehood will also be topics of discussion. The UK will convene a meeting on Gaza's current and future status, and Saudi Arabia and Norway will host a ministerial meeting to hash out plans for the implementation of the so-called "two-state solution."

Skip next section That's a wrap on Day 2 of the UNGA

That's a wrap on Day 2 of the UNGA

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russian President Vladimir Putin for the ongoing war between the countries, calling him "patient zero."

The Ukrainian leader also announced new defense deals with Finland and Australia.

Elsewhere, Syrian leader Ahmed al-Sharaa called for the Israeli occupation of the Golan Heights to end, saying the territory belongs to Syria.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also addressed Israel, calling for what he described as the "genocide" in Gaza to stop.

This comes ahead of a speech by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the UN General Assembly on Thursday.

Skip next section 'Too much power in too few hands' — AI leaders warn about technology dangers

'Too much power in too few hands' — AI leaders warn about technology dangers

Besides world leaders, top bosses at AI companies also addressed the UN about dangers concerning artificial intelligence.

AI executives spoke to the UN Security Council and urged international cooperation on the hotly debated technology.

Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, highlighted two big risks with AI.

"First, we could lose control of the future to AI. The risk is that it moves so fast that people can no longer follow what's happening or intervene when needed," he said, adding that such a scenario would be "terrible."

Second, he said AI systems "could concentrate too much power in too few hands." "No one person or company or country should be able to use the most powerful AI models to impose their worldview on everyone else."

Anthropic boss Dario Amodei used the platform to call for a ban on the use of AI in the development of biological weapons, describing AI as the most crucial global security issue facing the world.

"If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole," he said.

Amodei also urged global standards for testing new AI models.

Skip next section Spain PM Pedro Sanchez calls for reforming the UN Security Council

Spain PM Pedro Sanchez calls for reforming the UN Security Council

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchezcalled for reforming the UN Security Council so that "all of the regions in the world" would be fairly represented.

Sanchez quoted the UN Charter, saying "no country should be a judge in its own case, no matter how powerful they are."

The Spanish leader continued to condemn the "genocide that (Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin)  Netanyahu is still perpetrating in Gaza," while pointing to Madrid's sanctions against Russia as an example of his government's willingness to take action against countries whose conduct violates the UN Charter.

Skip next section Ebola outbreak 'major' test for country, Congo's PM tells UNGA

Ebola outbreak 'major' test for country, Congo's PM tells UNGA

Congolese Prime Minister ‌Judith ​Suminwa Tuluka described the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo as a "major test" for the country.

"For the DRC, fighting this epidemic is an absolute priority. After having contained ​16 previous outbreaks, the DRC is mobilizing recognized scientific and operational expertise. And thanks to national mobilization and the support of our

partners, the response has recently begun ​producing tangible results," she told the UN General Assembly.

As of 22 September 2026, Congo reported a total of 7, 773 confirmed cases, including 3,759 related deaths. A total of 839 patients are hospitalized in isolation.

Skip next section Venezuela to hold elections, Rodriguez tells UNGA

Venezuela to hold elections, Rodriguez tells UNGA

Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, delivered her first address to the UN General Assembly since coming to power, promising her country would hold elections when the nation's people determine the "right moment."

"I want to ‌make ⁠this very ⁠clear at this General Assembly: there will be elections in Venezuela," Rodriguez said, adding that her country "has initiated the process of democratic transformation for its rebirth" following two blows this year.

First, "strangulation of its internal political life and the heightened confrontation with the United States" and second, the earthquakes on June 24 that caused the deaths of more than 6,500 people.

Rodriguez took power after the US toppled the then-president Nicolas Maduro in January.

Rodríguez briefly met US President Donald Trump at the UN General Assembly as well.

Skip next section Ukrainian foreign minister met with Iranian delegation on the sidelines of UNGA

Ukrainian foreign minister met with Iranian delegation on the sidelines of UNGA

DW's US Correspondent Misha Komadovsky reported that the Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha met with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

Sybiah earlier in the day told a UN Security Council meeting that Ukraine was ready for an immediate and complete ceasefire without preconditions, if Moscow did too.

Skip next section German FM calls on Iran to end Hormuz blockage

German FM calls on Iran to end Hormuz blockage

In a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul called on Iran to end its closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

"It is up to Iran to engage constructively in negotiations and to loosen its stranglehold," Wadephul told journalists ahead of the meeting.

Wadephul also urged Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi to engage seriously and credibly in sustainable negotiations with the US and neighboring states in the region, sources in the German delegation were cited by the DPA news agency as saying.

"There must now be an overall willingness to compromise in order to bring about a solution to the deadlocked conflict in the region," Wadephul was quoted as saying.

He stressed the readiness of Germany and the so-called E3, which also includes France and the United Kingdom, to support mediation efforts.

Wadephul also stressed in the talks the need for Iran and militias it supports in the region, namely Yemen's Houthi rebels, to halt attacks on civilian ships. He added that Berlin expects free transit through the Strait of Hormuz to be restored immediately, stressing the rejection of any fees for passage through the critical waterway.

"Not only the Gulf States, but large parts of Asia, Africa and also Europe are suffering under this blockade," Wadephul said.

He added that Germany welcomes renewed talks between the US and Iran on the sidelines of the General Assembly, adding that he planned to speak to his counterparts from Jordan, Pakistan, Iraq and Oman.

Skip next section Zelenskyy announces defense deals with Finland, Australia

Zelenskyy announces defense deals with Finland, Australia

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also announced fresh deals with Finland and Australia related to defense, adding that another deal with Canada will follow.

Kyiv's defense experience against Russian drone strikes has now made it a world leader in the field.

"We are already working with partners in the Gulf, the South Caucasus, and across Europe through drone deals. Today, I signed a drone deal, a serious drone deal, with Finland," he said.

"Also today, I signed [a] security agreement with Australia, and drones are part of it too."

Skip next section Zelenskyy calls Putin 'patient zero,' from whom 'this idea of war keeps spreading further'

Zelenskyy calls Putin 'patient zero,' from whom 'this idea of war keeps spreading further'

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also addressed the ways the war in Ukraine had spread, not least North Korea sending troops to fight on Russia's behalf.

"Recently we sent two North Korean prisoners of war the the Republic of Korea," Zelenskyy said, referring to South Korea by its formal name. "And these guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, when he realized he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself." 

He said this spoke to how personnel in North Korea were trained and an attitude that "they must die, no matter what."

"Do you really want to give such a force more time to learn how to wage war?" he asked.

Zelenskyy said that North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un provided troops to Russia in a transactional way. He said he presumed North Korea's neighbors must have noticed what he said was the country's recently-improved missile capabilities. 

Zelenskyy alleged that Putin never seemed satisfied in his territorial ambitions and argued that this pattern applied beyond Ukraine.

He said that many around the world, in the south Caucasus, in Syria and across Africa "also know very well what Russian killers are." 

"After all of this, can you even imagine [Putin] without war?" Zelenskyy asked. "He is patient zero, the one from whom this idea of war keeps spreading further. And wherever it spreads, it brings only pain, instability, new risks and of course new crises."

The more space Putin has to operate, he argued, the more dangerous the world became for everyone else.

"That is why patient zero must be stopped. He must be denied the space to act and the space to spread this evil further," Zelenskyy said.

Skip next section Ukraine's Zelenskyy opens speech with critique of Putin, overture to Trump

Ukraine's Zelenskyy opens speech with critique of Putin, overture to Trump

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy opened his speech not just with a message targeting Russia after more than four and a half years of open war, but also aimed squarely at the sensibilities of his host in New York.

"This morning on my way to New York, somewhere in the sky over the big and beautiful Atlantic Ocean, I read President Trump's post on Truth Social," Zelenskyy began.

He relayed how Trump had written that Russia lost control of its diesel oil industry due to its war with Ukraine, an embarrassment for a UN Security Council member so proud of its oil industry.

"And this is true, Russia messed up," Zelenskyy said. "And the conclusion of the post is also right: this ridiculous and never-ending war with Ukraine must be ended. I do not know a single world leader who would say otherwise. I do not know anyone who is openly for this war: except one man."

He said that Russia had been trying to carry out what he called Putin's "crazy orders" to seize eastern Ukraine for more than four years.

"Just this year, from January through August" the Russian army "lost" 248,964 people on the battlefield in Ukraine, Zelenskyy said. He later clarified that this constituted military casualties — so soldiers "killed and badly wounded" and said "we have video confirmation for every one of these losses."

He said that amid these losses, Russia had only managed to capture "around 1,000 square kilometers (380 square miles) of our land this year," adding that "we have already liberated a significant part of it." He compared this to Russia's own vast territory spanning some 17 million square kilometers.

He said of the continued fighting: "It's madness, but they still keep going there to die, because that is what Putin wants."

entries.title: How renewed fighting in Tigray could spread across the Horn of Africa
entries.summary: The fresh hostilities in Ethiopia's Tigray region come after months of growing animosity between rebel forces and the federal government. Horn of Africa expert Martin Plaut warns of possible regional spillover.
entries.content:
Ethiopia

How Tigray's renewed fighting could spread in Horn of Africa

September 24, 2026

The fresh hostilities in Ethiopia's Tigray region come after months of growing animosity between rebel forces and the federal government. Horn of Africa expert Martin Plaut warns of possible regional spillover.

Fighting has erupted again in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Tigrayan forces launched a major offensive on September 23, with fighting also reported in the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara. 

The escalation threatens the fragile peace established by the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement, which ended the previous Tigray war between Ethiopia's federal government in Addis Ababa and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).

But the central question is bigger than the return of war to Tigray: could the conflict connect with the wars and rivalries already destabilizing the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea?

Martin Plaut, a British journalist and Horn of Africa expert, argues the conflict could spread beyond Ethiopia's borders.

"If a conflict were to spill over, it is quite possible that a conflict involving Eritrea and Ethiopia could then involve Sudanese forces as well, which could drag the whole region into a war," he told DW in an exclusive interview.

Jalale Getachew Birru, a senior analyst for East Africa at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), also stressed that the conflict cannot be viewed in isolation. ACLED is an independent conflict-monitoring and research organization that collects and analyzes data on political violence and armed conflict around the world.

“The Ethiopia[n] case is not [an] isolated case for the Horn of Africa. It involves the neighboring countries as well, and it's being displayed across the Horn of Africa countries," Birru told DW.

Her assessment points to a broader regional dynamic: Ethiopia's conflict is unfolding alongside shifting alliances and competing interests in neighboring Sudan and Somalia. ACLED's current analysis likewise places the renewed Tigray conflict within a wider pattern of instability across the Horn of Africa.

The risk is not based on a single regional alliance. It comes from the fact that several conflicts are already geographically and politically connected, Birru noted.

African Union urges restraint

The African Union (AU) has also expressed deep concern about the possibility of further destabilization.

In a statement on September 23, AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf warned that new political and military alliances risk reversing the progress made since 2020.

The AU called for an immediate end to actions that could escalate tensions, renewed direct talks under the Pretoria agreement and restraint by Ethiopia's neighbors. It also tasked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's high representative for the Horn of Africa, with supporting diplomatic efforts.

The AU's intervention reflects concerns that the crisis could have wider regional implications, including the possibility that it could interact with conflicts beyond Ethiopia's borders.

Old enemies, new alliances

The TPLF recently joined six other Ethiopian armed groups in an alliance seeking to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Among them is the Amhara Fano movement, which fought against the TPLF during the previous war.

The alliance is not a unified military force, and its members have different political objectives and territorial interests. But its formation could leave the Ethiopian government facing several fronts at once.

The fighting in Afar, a northeastern Ethiopian region bordering Eritrea and Djibouti, is particularly significant. The region contains the main transport corridor linking landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti, through which much of Ethiopia's international trade passes. Sustained fighting there could therefore threaten a vital economic lifeline.

And beyond Afar lies Eritrea.

Eritrea's potential role

During the 2020–2022 Tigray war, Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF. Since then, relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara, Eritrea's capital, have deteriorated. Ethiopia's ambitions for access to the Red Sea have added to Eritrea's security concerns.

"The war could certainly escalate, and Eritrea could become involved," Plaut said.

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups opposed to the government, while Asmara has denied such allegations. The extent of any direct Eritrean involvement remains difficult to establish independently.

Sudan: Where conflicts could collide

Sudan has been at war since 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict has drawn in regional powers and created one of the world's largest humanitarian crises.

Plaut argues that Ethiopia and Eritrea are already indirectly involved on opposing sides.

"The Ethiopians are on the side of the RSF and Hemedti," he said, referring to its commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo. "There has been strong evidence that there is a base in western Ethiopia which is supplying and training RSF fighters," Plaut added. DW has not independently verified that claim.

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has faced allegations of supporting the RSF, which it denies. Plaut identifies Eritrea, Egypt and Saudi Arabia as supporting the Sudanese Armed Forces.

"So both Eritrea and Ethiopia are already playing a role, indirectly, in the war," he said.

If Ethiopia and Eritrea were to enter direct hostilities, Sudan's rival forces could have incentives to exploit the new situation, Plaut said. Fighting could put additional pressure on Sudan's eastern frontier and alter supply routes and military calculations.

Plaut sees the danger of a chain reaction: "Because you have the UAE backing the RSF and you have the Saudis backing the Eritreans and the Sudanese Armed Forces, this could all multiply and you could get one conflict leading into another."

"So the whole thing becomes a generalized conflict in the region," he said.

Red Sea connection

The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most important shipping choke points, connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.

Eritrea and Djibouti lie on its western side, Yemen on the eastern side. The war in Yemen has already shown how insecurity around the Red Sea can disrupt international shipping and draw in outside powers.

Eritrea's location and its control of the port of Assab give it strategic importance far beyond Tigray. Any major deterioration in Ethiopia-Eritrea relations could therefore affect the wider security architecture of the Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia and the UAE have also developed extensive political, economic and security interests across the Horn of Africa. Their interests overlap in some areas but diverge in others, particularly over Sudan.

Danger is escalation, not inevitability

None of this means that a regional war is inevitable. There is no evidence of a single military alliance stretching from Tigray to the Gulf. Ethiopia's armed groups have competing interests, Eritrea may avoid direct intervention, and Sudan's warring parties have their own priorities.

But conflicts do not need a common command structure to become interconnected.

The Tigray war killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions. The Pretoria agreement stopped the large-scale fighting, but many of the political and territorial disputes underlying the conflict remained unresolved.

Today, Tigray is again at war while Ethiopia faces several armed movements, Eritrea is a potential military actor, and Sudan is already engulfed in civil war.

Plaut warns that the humanitarian consequences could again be severe.

"There's certainly a danger of this becoming an extremely bloody conflict," he told DW. "After all, 600,000 people died in the last one in Tigray."

But he does not predict that the previous death toll will necessarily be exceeded. "Let's hope that it doesn't go in that direction," he said.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: US-China talks on trade, AI between Trump, Xi beckon
entries.summary: The presidents of the world's two largest economies are in Washington for what Donald Trump has billed a "big day." Bilateral trade, AI and geopolitics are all on the menu. Follow DW for the latest.

The presidents of the world's two largest economies are in Washington for what Donald Trump has billed a "big day." Bilateral trade, AI and geopolitics are all on the menu. Follow DW for the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Donald Trump welcomed his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, to the White House
  • This is Xi's first state visit to the US in a decade
  • Trade, AI, Taiwan, Ukraine and Iran are key issues to be discussed

Follow along here for live updates on Xi's state visit to the US:

Skip next section CNN and MSNBC journalists are back at White House

CNN and MSNBC journalists are back at White House

Hours after a federal judge ordered Trump to lift the ban, US news outlets MSNBC and CNN announced that they had been granted access to the White House.

Politico journalists were also barred from the White House. The publication has not yet reported whether it has access again.

Skip next section Trump and Xi begin talks in Oval Office

Trump and Xi begin talks in Oval Office

After delivering their opening remarks and reviewing the military troops in the Rose Garden, Trump and Xi proceeded to the Oval Office for discussions.

Other US and Chinese officials joined them.

Skip next section China to send two pandas to Atlanta zoo, Xi says

China to send two pandas to Atlanta zoo, Xi says

Speaking at the White House, Xi Jinping announced that a pair of pandas will soon make their home at Zoo Atlanta.

This isn't the first time Chinese pandas have been sent to a U.S. zoo. It's also an example of what's known as "panda diplomacy." Through this program, China lends the animals to select zoos around the world.

Xi also revealed that Beijing plans to invite 100,000 young Americans to visit China for cultural exchange and study over the next five years.

Skip next section Xi thanks Trump for 'warm hospitality,' seeks to 'expand cooperation'

Xi thanks Trump for 'warm hospitality,' seeks to 'expand cooperation'

China's President Xi Jinping in turn thanked Donald Trump for his "warm hospitality," after the US president last night went to greet the Chinese leader and their wife on the tarmac at the airfeld.

In his opening remarks, as rendered by his interpreter, Xi said he was visiting the US to "carry on our friendship, expand cooperation and promote well-being of both our peoples."

He said that both the US and China were great countries with great people.

"I'm very glad to pay a state visit to your beautiful country, the United States of America," Xi said. "Thank you President Trump and Mrs. Trump for the warm hospitality that you have extended to me and my wife."

Skip next section Trump touts 'truly great friendship' with China's Xi, seeks more 'balanced' trade relationship

Trump touts 'truly great friendship' with China's Xi, seeks more 'balanced' trade relationship

The US president told reporters he was "proud" of the US-China relationship.

"From the time of my first election in 2016, President Xi and I have forged a friendship, a truly great friendship, actually, built on mutual respect and the vital interests of our people," Trump said.

He said that he and Xi would continue working together for a better future, while also hailing the "tremendous strides" he said had been made on issues facing the two countries.

Trump said that security, technology and artificial intelligence were likely to feature in Thursday's talks.

He said that US and Chinese officials were working to encourage a "more balanced" trading relationship between the two countries, including new market access for American farmers and ranchers.

Famously, Donald Trump tends to define "balance" in trade as not having an import surplus or trade deficit with a trading partner — a goal that can be particularly ambitious, bordering on impossible, when doing business with export giant China.

Skip next section Why is AI regulation in such sharp focus amid the visit?

Why is AI regulation in such sharp focus amid the visit?

With frozen tariff talks and moving deadlines, continued tensions over Taiwan and the Pacific region more generally, war in Iran, Ukraine, and much of Africa, you'd be forgiven for thinking that questions of hardware, software, bits and bytes would be far from the minds of the world's two most powerful politicians.

However, more and more examples of AI agents bending or breaking the rules they were given — coupled with increasing concern from the very people developing the models — have thrust the issue to the forefront of the public eye. 

At the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, various AI executives urged the UN Security Council and international governments to address some of the dangers concerning the technology. 

OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said there was a risk "we could lose control of the future to AI," because of its ability to move at such a rapid pace making human oversight difficult or impossible. He also said the systems could "concentrate too much power in too few hands."

Anthropic's boss Dario Amodei called for global standards for testing new AI models.

Compounding this, early on Thursday, Australia's Prime Minister Antony Albanese said that an Open AI agent had hacked Australia's public health data portal in June. It's the first known instance of AI hacking a government system, which is not necessarily to say it is the first. 

OpenAI said in response that its models "took actions we did not intend," in by no means the first case of its kind.

The US and China are seen as the two leading AI-developing nations, and have broadly advocated more of a hands-off approach to regulation than countries with less financial incentive to have tech companies on a long leash.

Skip next section Trump, First Lady welcome Xi, Madame Peng at White House

Trump, First Lady welcome Xi, Madame Peng at White House

China's President Xi Jinping and his wife have arrived at the White House to begin Thursday's talks.

They were greeted by US President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump outside the South Portico of the White House late on Thursday morning.

Skip next section Trump, Xi set for talks and a state dinner on Thursday

Trump, Xi set for talks and a state dinner on Thursday

Welcome back as police and security staff in Washington gear up for an even higher-profile day than usual on Thursday.

Talks between leaders of the US and China on Thursday are set to culminate in a state dinner at the White House this evening, attended by various tech executives.

US President Donald Trump told his online acolytes that a "big day with President Xi of China" beckoned in his first social media utterance on Thursday.

He said that artificial intelligence or machine learning would "be a big topic of discussion."

But, mirroring his comments at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump said he wanted to "leave it exactly where it is." 

He said that the US' "guardrail" for AI was its own Department of Justice, implying little interest in international or cooperative efforts to guard against any potential risks.

"That is China's position also," Trump asserted, though Xi Jinping is expected to deliver remarks of his own later.

Meanwhile, early morning reports from Washington suggest the White House was yet to react to the overnight court order demanding that it allow reporters from CNN, MSNOW and Politico back into the building, at least temporarily pending closer evalution of the case. 

Skip next section We're pausing our coverage for now

We're pausing our coverage for now

The main summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping is scheduled for Thursday.

There's a state dinner as well in the evening, with both leaders expected to deliver speeches.

Top US tech executives are expected to attend the dinner, suggesting that artificial intelligence will be a big topic of discussion.

Skip next section China, US should be 'partners rather than rivals' — Xi

China, US should be 'partners rather than rivals' — Xi

Chinese President Xi Jinping has called for cooperation with the US, Beijing's state news agency Xinhua reported.

"Our two countries should be partners rather than rivals," Xi said in a written statement published by Xinhua.

"The Chinese and US peoples have enjoyed long-standing friendly exchanges, and our interests are deeply intertwined," Xi added.

Xi was welcomed in Washington with a red carpet and military flyover.

In remarks published by Xinhua, Xi also said he looked forward to "in-depth exchanges" with Trump on "major issues concerning our bilateral relations and the global situation."

Skip next section Trump wants Hong Kong's Jimmy Lai to be freed from prison — report

Trump wants Hong Kong's Jimmy Lai to be freed from prison — report

Chinese President Xi Jinping has arrived in Washington to a rare planeside welcome from his US counterpart, Donald Trump. 

As Xi walked down a long red carpet on the airport tarmac, a White House spokesperson said that Trump believes Hong Kongdemocracy advocate Jimmy Lai should be released from prison and "wants to see that happen," the DPA news agency reported.

"The United States urges the authorities to grant Mr. Lai humanitarian parole," DPA quoted the spokesperson as saying.

Lai, a 78-year-old media tycoon, was sentenced to 20 years in prison earlier in the year under the National Security Law that China imposed in 2020 following massive pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong. 

At a congressional hearing in Washington last week, Lai's son, Sebastien, repeated his appeal for his father's release.

Trump raised the issue of Lai's release when he met Xi in Beijing in May, but the US leader said the Chinese president told him Lai's case "would be a tough one."

On Tuesday, US outlet Politico reported that British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked Trump to discuss the release of Lai, who is a British citizen, with Xi.

Skip next section US, China to extend trade truce through January 2, Scott Bessent says

US, China to extend trade truce through January 2, Scott Bessent says

The US and China have agreed to extend their trade truce by two months, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.

The announcement came as Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington to meet with US President Donald Trump.

"We have agreed today that we will extend what we call the Busan Agreement, the economic detente between the two countries that was scheduled to end on November 10th," Bessent told Fox News.

The extension of the one-year trade truce buys both sides more time to negotiate.

Skip next section IN PHOTOS: Trump welcomes China's Xi to United States

IN PHOTOS: Trump welcomes China's Xi to United States

Skip next section Trump hosts Xi in Washington: What to expect

Trump hosts Xi in Washington: What to expect

Chinese President Xi Jinping's plane landed in Washington for his state visit to the US, which will include a meeting and state dinner with  Donald Trump on Thursday.

Unlike with other leaders, Trump honored Xi by welcoming him at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington rather than waiting for him at the White House.

The greeting, which included a red carpet lined by US service members and a military flyover, kicks off the Chinese leader's three-day visit to Washington.

Additional fanfare during the trip is due to include a state dinner with tech executives and a visit to the National Archives, where the original Declaration of Independence and Constitution are housed.

Expectations for a breakthrough during Xi's visit were slim.

Despite their deep disagreements, the two world leaders went ahead with their summit that analysts say is meant to project stability on the world stage.

The issues the two will discuss are expected to include trade, artificial intelligence, as well as the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

Xi will also likely press Trump on Taiwan, a topic Washington would prefer to avoid, while Trump will likely maintain firm US export controls despite Xi's objections. 

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

We are launching our coverage of the highly anticipated meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.

Trade, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and artificial intelligence are expected to be on the agenda as the two leaders hold their main meeting on Thursday.

This is Xi's first state visit to Washington in a decade.

Join us for updates from Xi's trip.

entries.title: EU to condemn war in Ukraine at G20 even if Putin attends
entries.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin has been invited to the G20 summit in Miami by the United States. Multiple members of the group have called for Moscow's exclusion over its invasion of Ukraine.
entries.content:
Ukraine

EU to condemn war in Ukraine at G20 even if Putin attends

September 24, 2026

Russian President Vladimir Putin has been invited to the G20 summit in Miami by the United States. Multiple members of the group have called for Moscow's exclusion over its invasion of Ukraine.

The European Union said on Thursday that it would continue to condemn Russia's war in Ukraine at the G20 summit in Miami scheduled for December.

It said that it would do this regardless of whether Russian President Vladimir Putin attends after being invited by this year's hosting country, the United States. The Kremlin has said that Putin would "consider" Washington's invitation.

The Russian leader did not attend the G20 summit in 2023 in New Delhi, India and the 2022 summit on the Indonesian island of Bali despite being formally invited by the hosting countries.

Also on Thursday, eight people were killed in a wave of Russian strikes on Ukraine.

What did the EU say about Putin's possible attendance at the G20 summit?

The EU said it would continue calling for an end to the war in Ukraine.

"Since 2022, the EU has consistently and forcefully used G20 meetings to condemn Russia's full-scale invasion [of Ukraine] and to call for it to end," EU spokesman Olof Gill said.

"What I can say today is that this approach, from the European Union perspective, will continue, irrespective of the participants at any G20 meeting."

Gill said that Russia remained a member of the G20 group and that it had "the right to participate" in its meetings.

Both the European Union itself and three of its individual member states — France, Germany, and Italy — are members of the G20 group.

What is the US position on Putin's attendance at the G20?

Ukraine's allies — including G20 members France, Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom and Canada — have called for Russia's exclusion from the group since Moscow launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that Washington was inviting Putin after his meeting with his Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

"We think it's an opportunity for him to engage not just with [US President Donald Trump], but with other world leaders," Rubio said on Wednesday. "We hope that's an invitation he'll accept."

Putin's last visit to the United States was to attend a summit meeting with Trump in Anchorage, Alaska in August 15, 2025, also marking his first visit to a Western country since the start of the war in Ukraine.

Russian strikes kill 8 in Kharkiv, Kyiv

At least six agricultural workers were killed and 12 others were wounded in a strike on the northeastern Ukrainian region of Kharkiv, Interior Minister Ihor Vyhivskyi said.

The regional prosecutor's office published images showing the inside of a destroyed warehouse following the attack.

Ukrainian authorities said that the warehouse had been hit by a small-sized cruise missile of the "Banderol" type.

Meanwhile, at least two people were killed across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, Prime Minsiter Serhiy Koretsky said.

Strikes were also recorded in and around the southwestern port city of Odesa, with officials reporting they sparked a fire at a shopping mall.

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google so you'll always see our verified news first.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Could flattering AI make humanity turn on itself?
entries.summary: A study shows chatbots mirror users' politics, part of a broader tendency known as AI sycophancy. Researchers fear this could deepen polarization.
entries.content:
September 24, 2026

A study shows chatbots mirror users' politics, part of a broader tendency known as AI sycophancy. Researchers fear this could deepen polarization.

A recent wave of headline-grabbing warnings from AI luminaries has fueled fears that the technology could escape human control and wipe out humanity. But before artificial intelligence (AI) turns on humanity, it could contribute to humans turning on one another.

Researchers at Brazil's State University of Campinas (UNICAMP) found that popular chatbots shifted their answers when prompted with hypothetical users' political views. The scientists warn that users could mistake this tailored agreement for an independent assessment, potentially deepening polarization.

How chatbots become 'ideological chameleons'

In their study published in the journal Scientific Reports, the UNICAMP team tested 21 large language models from developers including OpenAI, Meta, Google, xAI, DeepSeek and Microsoft.



The models rated their agreement with 112 statements covering seven areas of Brazilian politics, including the economy, public safety, welfare, corruption and the environment.

Each was tested under three conditions: with no information about the user's politics, with a prompt describing a left-leaning user and with one describing a right-leaning user.

When no information about the user's ideology was given, 20 of the 21 models produced answers that fell on the left of the researchers' political scale, although several were close to the center. Grok 4.1 was the only model that fell on the right.

When information was provided, every model shifted its answers toward the political orientation described in the prompt.

"The most striking finding was how widespread this behavior was," study co-author Zanoni Dias, a UNICAMP computer scientist, told DW. "All 21 models we evaluated shifted their expressed positions toward the user's stated political orientation, although the magnitude varied substantially."

The researchers described the models as "ideological chameleons" and developed a "chameleon index" measuring how far each shifted.

Meta's Llama 3.1 8B and DeepSeek V3.2 changed their responses least. Google's Gemma 3 27B and OpenAI's GPT-5 Nano showed some of the largest shifts.

When personalization becomes political flattery

Adapting an answer to its audience is not inherently problematic. A chatbot might change its vocabulary, examples or level of detail depending on the user.

But the models changed more than their language or tone: Their political positions shifted.

"The key distinction is between adapting how an answer is communicated and changing the substantive judgment being expressed," Dias said.

"We did not instruct the models to agree with the user or to answer as a partisan representative. Nevertheless, their judgments shifted toward the user's side."

The researchers interpret this as political sycophancy: AI systems reflecting what users appear to want to hear.

A possible explanation is that chatbots are trained to favor answers human evaluators rate highly. If agreeable answers get better ratings, models may learn to echo users' views.

How AI could create a private echo chamber

Social media can reinforce beliefs by repeatedly recommending algorithmic content, but a chatbot could go even further. It could create a more personalized echo chamber, generating arguments for a particular user, answering their objections and refining its case throughout the conversation.

Yet users may mistake these tailored responses for impartial analysis, unaware that what a chatbot knows about them may shape its responses.

"The concern is that the same system could validate opposing political positions for different users, with each person interpreting that validation as an independent assessment," Dias said.

Research by Stanford University behavioral scientist Zakary Tormala suggests people may be particularly receptive to arguments they believe came from AI.

"People tend to see AI as more informative, more objective, less biased and less interested in persuading them than another person would be," Tormala told DW. "This can lower people's defenses and make them more receptive to hearing out what AI has to say."

That trust could make political flattery more influential.

"Hearing their own views validated by others is well known to increase people's certainty about their beliefs," Tormala said. "Once people become more certain, they do tend to become more resistant to persuasion."

Whether AI validation has the same effect remains unproven, he added, but it is plausible.

Could validation deepen polarization?

The UNICAMP study did not test whether political mirroring could really change users' beliefs or behavior. It measured only changes in the models' responses.

"Our study establishes a change in model responses under controlled conditions," Dias said. "It does not establish that users became more polarized, radicalized or likely to engage in conflict. Those are distinct outcomes, and the steps connecting them cannot be assumed."

Petter Tornberg, a University of Amsterdam researcher who studies AI and political polarization, agreed that the study cannot show an effect on users. He also questioned whether models would give the same answers outside the test setting.

He cautioned against assuming that chatbots would necessarily reinforce users’ views. In some conversations, they might help people reconsider them.

Tornberg said a private conversation with a chatbot differs from a public argument on social media.

"They can often provide fairly rational and evidence-based explanations without the social identity dynamics of public political debate," he told DW. "So it is at least possible that in some contexts these systems could be depolarizing rather than polarizing."

Whether AI narrows or deepens divisions may therefore depend on whether it challenges users or simply tells them what they want to hear.

How political mirroring could be reduced

Dias said developers should test their models with users of different political views to see whether they assess evidence consistently.

They could train models to disagree respectfully, acknowledge uncertainty, correct unsupported claims and present competing views fairly.

That would not mean forcing every answer toward the political center.

"The broader design goal should be to help people examine their beliefs," Dias said, "making evidence, uncertainty and competing considerations visible, while allowing room for legitimate political disagreement."

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

entries.title: Germany news: Berlin officially withdraws Olympics bid
entries.summary: Berlin's decision to withdraw its Olympic bid means that only Munich and the western Rhine/Ruhr region are left in the running as potential Olympic hosts. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Berlin officially withdraws Olympics bid

Published September 24, 2026last updated September 24, 2026

Berlin's decision to withdraw its Olympic bid means that only Munich and the western Rhine/Ruhr region are left in the running as potential Olympic hosts. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Berlin has confirmed reports that it is withdrawing its bid to host the Summer Olympics and Paralympics.
  • Lawmakers debate whether to introduce an opt-out scheme for organ donation
  • The Bundestag will also examine government proposals to grant intelligence agencies a wider scope to counter manifold security threats
  • German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has warned of Russia's growing aggression against Europe
  • The first-ever Islamic theology faculty in Germany is to open in Münster

Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Thursday, September 24, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Far-left German activist Lina E. freed again after refusing to testify

Far-left German activist Lina E. freed again after refusing to testify

A German woman convicted of attacking far-right activists will be released from detention following a ruling by the Federal Constitutional Court.

A court spokeswoman confirmed that the woman, identified only as Lina E. due to German privacy laws, will be released pending a final decision.

Lina E. was originally sentenced to five years and three months in prison in May 2023 for serious assault and forming a criminal association. She and her accomplices were accused of carrying out several attacks against suspected members of far-right groups in the eastern states of Saxony and Thuringia between 2018 and 2020.

Her conviction sparked outrage among left-wing activists and led to riots in several cities across Germany, most notably in Leipzig.

After serving two-thirds of her sentence, she was released on probation in May in a ruling by the Federal Court of Justice.

However, in June, she was jailed for six months by a Dresden court after refusing to testify in a case involving the far-left Antifa-Ost group.

Skip next section German Defense Ministry declines comment on reported CIA drone warning

German Defense Ministry declines comment on reported CIA drone warning

A German Defense Ministry spokesperson declined to comment on media reports that the CIA had warned of potential Russian drone attacks targeting Spain, France and Italy.

Asked by DW what the warning means for Germany, the spokesperson said the ministry generally does not comment on media reports. However, the spokesperson said European Union (EU) and NATO members routinely share intelligence through bilateral channels, EU operations and NATO's integrated air and missile defense framework.

German military units and institutions also contribute on an ongoing basis to creating a shared situational picture, the spokesperson added.

Citing a source close to the Lithuanian Ministry of Defense, Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported that the US intelligence agency has warned Russia is preparing to carry out drone strikes in Europe targeting France, Spain and Italy from the sea.

It comes in the wake of a string of drone incidents near sensitive sites elsewhere in Europe, including Belgium, Germany and Denmark.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Could Berlin expropriate large real estate companies?

IN DEPTH: Could Berlin expropriate large real estate companies?

The socialist Left Party won the Berlin election partly on the promise to implement the city's 2021 expropriation referendum to address the city's rent crisis. But can it really happen?

Skip next section German business confidence up in September — Ifo

German business confidence up in September — Ifo

The monthly business climate index put out by the Ifo economic research institute has risen 1.1 points to 89.9 points, the highest level in more than three years.

The index, Germany's most important economic barometer, has been rising constantly over the past five months, indicating that the country is slowly returning to economic health after years of struggle.

The business optimism comes despite an energy price ​shock that has pushed fuel costs to record highs.

"The German economy continues its recovery," said Ifo president Clemens Fuest.

The ​gauge of business expectations accompanying the index rose to 90.4 ​from 89.1 in August, while companies also gave a rosier assessment of their current situation than the month before, improving to 89.5 to 88.5 points.

Ifo said, however, that the automotive sector was still in "difficult terrain."  

The index is based on a monthly survey of 9,000 companies.

The news from Ifo comes as ​the country's five leading economic institutes presented a joint fall forecast raising 2026 GDP growth expectations to 1.3% from ⁠0.6%.

Skip next section 105-year-old suspected Nazi POW guard under investigation

105-year-old suspected Nazi POW guard under investigation

German prosecutors said on Thursday that they were investigating a 105-year-old man over crimes that might have been committed during his alleged time as a guard at a Nazi prisoner-of-war camp during World War II.

In a statement seen by the AFP news agency, they said the man was "thought to have been a guard at the prisoner-of-war camp Stalag 326 VI K" in the Senne region of western Germany.

The man is "accused of being an accessory to multiple murders through his activities there," the statement said.

The Stalag 326 VI K camp held between 180,000 and 200,000 Soviet prisoners of war between 1941 and April 1945, when it was liberated by US troops, according to the memorial at the site.

Some 30,000 Soviet POWs are believed to have died at the camp.

The age of the suspect is a reminder that time is running out to prosecute people who committed crimes as part of Germany's Nazi regime.

In April 2025,  for example, an alleged former guard at the Sachsenhausen concentration camp near Berlin died before he could face trial on charges of complicity in the murder of more than 3,300 people.

Skip next section Berlin officially withdraws Olympics bid

Berlin officially withdraws Olympics bid

Berlin has confirmed reports that it is withdrawing its bid to host the Summer Olympics and Paralympics.

The decision means that only Munich and the western Rhine/Ruhr region are still in the running as potential hosts, with Hamburg having pulled out in May after failing to win support at a referendum. 

The withdrawal comes after the socialist Left Party's victory in Berlin's elections on Sunday. The party's lead candidate and potential mayor, Elif Eralp, said she did not support Berlin's bid.

The current mayor, Kai Wegner of the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), told reporters: "Today is a sad day for Berlin, because the Olympic and Paralympic Games would have been a tremendous opportunity."

"When Ms. Eralp stated that the bid was effectively off the table ... the leading sports associations made it clear: We cannot give you our approval under these circumstances," he said, adding: "I deeply regret this."

Kaweh Niroomand, the volleyball manager who led the Berlin bid, said, "We simply could not offer the political stability required."

On Saturday, the German Olympic Committee (DOSB) is to choose a preferred region as part of a bid to the International Olympic Committee to host one of the 2036, 2040 and 2044 Summer Games.

The Summer Olympics have been held twice on German soil.

Berlin hosted the Games in 1936 in then Nazi-ruled Germany and Munich, then as part of West Germany, was the site of the 1972 Games.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Top economic think tanks raise 2026 GDP growth forecasts

IN DEPTH: Top economic think tanks raise 2026 GDP growth forecasts

Economic experts predicted on Thursday that German GDP will double to 1.3% this year. They also warned of difficulties ahead.

You can read more about their forecasts for Germany's economic future in the next few years in this article: Germany: Economic institutes double growth forecast for 2026

Skip next section Planned intelligence reforms trigger heated Bundestag debate

Planned intelligence reforms trigger heated Bundestag debate

The German parliament has held its first debate on government plans to give intelligence agencies more power as national security is threatened by new dangers at home and from abroad.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told parliamentarians that the planned reforms would turn Germany's intelligence agencies — the BND (Bundesnachrichtendienst), in charge of international intelligence, and the BfV (Bundesamt für Verfassungschutz), responsible for domestic intelligence — into "true secret services."

He said the agencies would no longer just gather information on threats but be equipped to provide "real defense against dangers, attacks and terror."

Under the plans, the agencies would receive more power to collect, save and automatically evaluate data, as well as permission to react to sabotage or hacking attacks with counterattacks.

Intelligence reforms under fire

Various parliamentarians voiced concerns about the reform's implications in what was sometimes a heated discussion.

Konstantin von Notz from the Green Party said he recognized the need to "update" the powers of the agencies in view of the growing threat from Russia.

But, he said, "the excessive plans for domestic intelligence activities" needed to be trimmed or the the reforms would not survive an appeal to the Constitutional Court.

He said the government needed to take the interests of people professionally entrusted with confidential information much more into consideration, especially psychotherapists.

Clara Bünger of the socialist Left Party accused the government of breaking down the distinction between intelligence agencies and the police that had been a lesson learned "from the crimes of the German fascists."

The far-right politician Gottfried Curio from the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party was strongest in his criticism, saying the government wanted to create a "Stasi 2.0," a reference to the secret service in former communist East Germany.   

The reforms would bring about "more than a total surveillance state," he said.

Skip next section Bundestag set for organ donation debate

Bundestag set for organ donation debate

The Bundestag will discuss two separate cross-party proposals on Thursday to increase the number of human organs donated for often life-saving transplant operations.

One proposal upholds Germany's current system, under which people who wish to donate organs must actively give permission.

Advocates of the proposal say that the shortfall of donated organs can be remedied by campaigns calling on adults to take part and making it easier to register the desire to donate.

The other proposal calls for an opt-out scheme under which organs can be removed postmortem from anyone who has not expressly rejected being an organ donor.

Backers of this proposal say that although surveys show that most people in Germany are willing to donate their organs, very few actually document this wish.

They also cite statistics showing that countries with opt-out schemes have more donations, with Germany lagging behind in international comparisons.

Altogether 254 of the 630 members of the Bundestag have signed on to the opt-out scheme, and 58 have backed the first proposal to maintain the current national system.

The Bundestag last voted on the issue in 2020, with a majority supporting the opt-in model, even though an opt-out proposal had more signees then, too.

France, Spain and the Netherlands are examples of European countries that have opt-out models in place.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The DW newsroom in Bonn says guten Tag and willkommen to its readers around the world!

You join our coverage as the German parliament is set to revisit a debate on organ donations: Should an opt-out scheme replace the current opt-in one in view of the dwindling supply?

Parliamentarians will also be looking at goverment proposals to give more powers to the country's intelligence agencies to enable them to cope with the current myriad of security threats.

And the university in Münster is to open a faculty of Islamic theology — the first in the country — that will have an equal status with the Catholic and Protestant faculties there.

All this comes amid a bit of good news for the German economy, which experts say will grow twice as much this year as previously forecast.

Read on for more on these and other stories.

entries.title: Czech PM Andrej Babis reiterates importance of NATO for his country but rejects calls to increase defense spending
entries.summary: The US and NATO want Czechia to spend more on defense. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis says Prague cannot afford faster increases, despite growing warnings about the threat from Russia.
entries.content:
Czech Republic

Czech PM Babis under fire for missing NATO spending targets

September 24, 2026

The US and NATO want Czechia to spend more on defense. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis says Prague cannot afford faster increases, despite growing warnings about the threat from Russia.

The Czech Republic "must remain committed to increasing defense spending," Matthew Whitaker, the US envoy to NATO, demanded in Prague last week. "We ⁠expect our allies to step up," he said.

The call is nothing new. As warnings about the threat emanating from Russia increase, and Washington demands European allies take greater responsibility for security, NATO has raised its target for defense spending from 2% to 3.5% of GDP, and pressure on those lagging is rising. 

Czechia, alongside Slovenia and Albania, has yet to meet the old target. But Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, whose government cut the defense budget for 2026 to around 1.7% of GDP when it took office late last year, pushed back against the latest barb from Washington. 

While reiterating that NATO membership is crucial for Czechia, the premier bluntly stated that the government cannot afford to accelerate spending. He has pledged to hit the 2% target in 2027 but plans no further increases.

That leaves the populist billionaire hoping that a personal rapport with US President Donald Trump will protect the country amid the burgeoning row.

Warnings of a growing threat

Whether Trump will protect Czechia from the threat of Russian hybrid warfare targeting Central European NATO allies is another question.

A growing wave of stray drones and Russian intelligence operations — suspected bombings, sabotage and cyber warfare — have spread alarm in the neighborhood.

Germany and Poland — key Czech partners — have reported high-profile incidents and linked them to attempts to intimidate Ukrainian allies.

Czechia should understand the threat better than most, having been among the first to experience such an attack.

Czechia's Security Information Service (BIS) reported in 2021 that the bombing of a depot storing weapons linked to Ukraine seven years previously had been carried out by Russia's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Security Service (FSB).

Babis, then in his first stint as PM, responded by expelling around 100 Russian diplomats and embassy staff, freezing relations with Moscow.

The BIS remains in step with other intelligence agencies across the region in warning that the threat from Russia is growing.

However, like its predecessors, the Babis government has failed to keep pace in terms of the national defense budget, even as neighbors have leapt into action.

Prague spent just 1.86% of GDP on defense last year; Poland and the Baltic States have already met the new NATO target and will hit 5% next year.

Prague's priorities

Babis has made it clear this approach will not change. However, his claim that Czechia can't afford to boost defense spending is at odds with the 2027 budget his government approved on September 22.

The fiscal plan will expand expenditure generously and targets Czechia's second-highest deficit ever at 386 billion Czech crowns (€15.8 billion or $18 billion).

While finally catching up to the old NATO target will account for some of that spending, most of the increased outlay will reflect the coalition government's domestic political priorities.

The plan clearly reflects the election campaign promises of Babis's ANO party and its junior partners, the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD) and radical-right Motorists for Themselves party. They all say defense can't be allowed to disrupt the urgent need to spend on pensions, education, healthcare and infrastructure.

"The claim that the country cannot spend more on defense is primarily rooted in domestic politics," Ales Michal, a political scientist at Prague's Charles University, told DW. "The major priority is investment in the social system."

That will be welcomed by supporters of the governing parties, who skew older and less well off, and resent the support being given to 300,000 or so Ukrainian refugees.

"None of the governing parties promised voters higher defense spending," in campaigning for last year's election, Michal notes.

Critics, however, say that's because the government is downplaying the threat from Russia. The government's spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

'We don't want World War III'

The reticence to raise defense spending also reflects political narratives around the war in Ukraine.

Two days after Whitaker's rebuke, Babis appeared in a video dressed in a T-shirt emblazoned with the words "No War" in blue and yellow letters. While he noted the threat from Russia, he called for greater efforts to find peace.

"We don't want World War III, do we?" he pronounced, repeating his claim that Europe should work harder to end the conflict.

It was a performance echoing the stance of Europe's radical right-wing, and the sort that has seen the Czech PM labelled "pro-Russian" in some international media.

The truth is more mundane. Babis is a pragmatist. The ANO electorate is populist and anti-Ukrainian, but also strongly pro-Western. Surveys show that the plan to keep defense spending at 2% of GDP precisely matches its views.

Yet Babis's divisive personality leaves the party dependent on extremist partners for enough support to govern, and so he must also try to speak the anti-system, pro-Russian language of the SPD, which, despite controlling the defense ministry, was pushing to cut spending further in the 2027 budget.

"A critical stance towards Ukraine also shapes the government's position on spending," said Michal. The pro-peace stance downplaying Russia's aggression moves ANO "closer to the European radical right," he notes, but Babis is "guided by opinion polls," and must try to find a "balance between two polarizing positions."

Strategic understanding

The opposition sees this dichotomy as the government's Achilles' heel.

Martin Kupka, leader of the center-right Civic Democrats (ODS), welcomed Babis's reiterated NATO commitment before asking the PM: "When will you get rid of the Kremlin fifth column, which you took into the government and even entrusted with the Ministry of Defense?"

However, although the ODS-led government that held office between 2021 and 2025 offered fervent support to Ukraine, like all its predecessors, it also failed to meet the NATO spending target.

"Our partners may be unhappy about the approach to spending, but it's the reality of the political situation in our country," Andor Sandor, a defense analyst and former commander of Czechia's Military Intelligence Service, told DW.

However, he added that while weak defense spending growth "is not optimal," the biggest issue is a lack of strategic understanding regarding the military's size and role.
